proposals.evidence_note: Own2005interview240 explicitly credits reading Bloch and Febvre within that formation, while distinguishing Braudel. The recollection also preserves his later methodological disagreements; no named Bloch book or exclusive lineage is invented. Whole original works unread.

proposals.relationship: Veyne recalls Febvre’s writing as part of his formative immersion in the Annales approach.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005interview240 names Febvre alongside Bloch and explicitly distinguishes Braudel. Reading debt and later Annales criticism coexist; this is not a claim that Veyne adopted all of Febvre’s positions or was his student. Whole cited works unread.

proposals.relationship: Veyne identifies Weber among the thinkers from whom he learned most, defending the use of German theory in his historical work.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2005interview237contrasts limited learning from Bourdieu with Weber,Aron and Passeron;241recalls using Weber and Simmel despite Braudel’s reported objection. This is Veyne’s selected retrospective, not proof of a particular German edition or a fresh reading of Weber’s original works. The other thinkers retain credit.

proposals.relationship: Acknowledges Nietzsche’s treatment of truth in an extra-moral sense as a resource for thinking about the human need for truth (2005).
proposals.evidence_note: Own replies238–239 explicitly identify Nietzsche’s opening biological thought experiment and discuss a translation point. Interviewer parallels with Searle,Quine and Winnicott remain separately attributed. Nietzsche’s original and the noted bilingual1969French edition are unread; no whole-work nihilist affiliation is inferred.

proposals.relationship: Uses Foucault’s analyses of self-government and conduct to interpret imperial legitimacy and political subjectivation in Roman history (1985–86).
proposals.evidence_note: Own course report719and724 explicitly invokes Foucault. The2005interview240–243also values his historical conceptual resources, alongside Passeron’s theory of semi-proper names. The earlier course witness supports an actual use; it does not infer general dependence from friendship or retrofit Foucault into the1971book.

proposals.relationship: Invokes Geertz’s thick description as a way to test historical interpretation through a more fully described context (2005).
proposals.evidence_note: Own reply244, prompted by a question about proof, expressly admits knowing only fragments of Geertz’s account. Preserve that limited acquaintance; this is not a claim of a complete Geertz reading or wholesale interpretive-anthropology commitment. Original cited works unread.

proposals.relationship: Questions the predictive and conceptual expectations associated with Annales interdisciplinarity while acknowledging the school’s formative and heuristic value (2005 retrospect).
proposals.evidence_note: Own240–242 distinguishes hard-science concepts from historically situated ideal types and criticizes the school’s assumptions. His critique coexists with his Bloch/Febvre reading debt and explicit praise for the school’s repertoire of questions. Not a blanket rejection of interdisciplinary history or evidence that all Annales historians held a single doctrine.

proposals.relationship: Veyne recalls Braudel objecting to his use of German theoretical resources, specifically Weber and Simmel.
proposals.evidence_note: Veyne’s own2005recollection241 of a letter; the original correspondence is unread and undated here. The claim is expressly recipient-reported, not independently collated Braudel words or a blanket opposition to German scholarship. Preserve Veyne’s separate acknowledgment of the Annales context.
